title: Tulunids
capsule: The Tulunid dynasty, founded by Ahmad ibn Tulun (r. 868–884), was the first autonomous Muslim dynasty to rule Egypt since the Arab conquest, though nominally remaining within the Abbasid caliphate. Ibn Tulun, a Turkic military commander sent as deputy governor, progressively seized fiscal and military control, built the new city of al-Qata'i north of Fustat as his capital—including the surviving Ibn Tulun Mosque—and extended his authority into Syria and the Jazira. His son Khumarawayh consolidated these gains and in 886 extracted formal recognition of hereditary rule over Egypt and Syria from Caliph al-Mu'tamid in exchange for tribute. The dynasty collapsed rapidly after Khumarawayh's assassination in 896: three sons succeeded in quick succession, and in 905 the Abbasid general Muhammad ibn Sulayman reconquered Egypt, razed al-Qata'i, and ended Tulunid rule.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. Egypt's extent under the Tulunids is clearly attested; their Syrian and Jaziran holdings fluctuated and are reconstructed principally from Arabic chronicles with limited cartographic corroboration.
